etymology: From Canaan, the son of Ham and grandson of Noah (Genesis 9:22, 10:6), whose descendants settled the land between the Jordan and the Great Sea. Webster 1828 has CANAANITE, a descendant of Canaan, an inhabitant of the land of Canaan. In Scripture the word carries at once a genealogy, a geography, and a verdict: the Canaanites are the people whose iniquity filled up the measure God had set, and whose land was given to Abraham’s seed by covenant grant.
biblical_def: The Canaanites are the settled inhabitants of the land promised to Abraham, named first in the table of nations and last in the Gospels. They head the standing list of the doomed peoples: the Amorites, and the Canaanites, and the Girgashites, and the Jebusites (Genesis 15:21), and again in the sevenfold roll of Deuteronomy 7:1. The Lord did not hide His reason for the four-hundred-year delay: the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet full (Genesis 15:16). Canaan was not seized from the innocent; it was taken from a civilization that had ripened in child sacrifice, temple prostitution, and the abominations catalogued in Leviticus 18. The conquest was a judicial act of the Judge of all the earth, executed through Israel as His instrument, and Israel was warned in the same breath that the same land would vomit her out for the same sins (Leviticus 18:28). Israel did not finish the work. The children of Israel dwelt among the Canaanites (Judges 3:5), and the leaven of that tolerated remnant runs through the whole book of Judges and out into the monarchy. Yet Scripture will not let the category harden into race. Rahab the Canaanite is in the genealogy of Christ, and a Canaanite mother in Matthew 15:22 gets from the Son of David what Israel’s own elders would not ask for.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines CANAANITE as a descendant of Canaan, the son of Ham, and an inhabitant of the land of Canaan; he notes the secondary use of the word for a trafficker or merchant, which follows the Hebrew idiom itself.
webster_full: CANAANITE, n. — A descendant of Canaan, the son of Ham; an inhabitant of the land of Canaan, afterward called Palestine.
The Hebrew word came also to signify a merchant or trafficker, from the Canaanite’s trade along the coast — a sense the prophets use pointedly (Hosea 12:7; Zephaniah 1:11).
The plural denotes collectively the peoples dispossessed by Israel under Joshua, of whom seven nations are named in Deuteronomy 7:1.
Webster’s entry is purely descriptive, as the 1828 lexicon usually is with proper nouns; the moral weight of the word is supplied entirely by Scripture.

That the same root should mean both Canaanite and merchant is a small witness to how the ancient world knew these people: by their harbors and their trade, long before Israel knew them by their altars.
scriptures: Genesis 15:16
But in the fourth generation they shall come hither again: for the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet full.
Deuteronomy 7:1

When the LORD thy God shall bring thee into the land whither thou goest to possess it, and hath cast out many nations before thee, the Hittites, and the Girgashites, and the Amorites, and the Canaanites, and the Perizzites, and the Hivites, and the Jebusites, seven nations greater and mightier than thou;
Judges 3:5
And the children of Israel dwelt among the Canaanites, Hittites, and Amorites, and Perizzites, and Hivites, and Jebusites:
Joshua 24:11

And ye went over Jordan, and came unto Jericho: and the men of Jericho fought against you, the Amorites, and the Perizzites, and the Canaanites, and the Hittites, and the Girgashites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites; and I delivered them into your hand.
Matthew 15:22
And, behold, a woman of Canaan came out of the same coasts, and cried unto him, saying, Have mercy on me, O Lord, thou Son of David; my daughter is grievously vexed with a devil.
corruption_summary: The conquest of the Canaanites is the standard modern charge against the God of the Old Testament — called genocide by the New Atheists and quietly disowned by progressive evangelicals who prefer a Jesus detached from the Judge of Genesis 15.
corruption_paragraphs: The charge that the conquest was genocide reads a judicial sentence as an ethnic policy. Genesis 15:16 settles the question of motive: the delay of four centuries was mercy, and the execution came only when the iniquity of the Amorites was full. Leviticus 18 names what filled it. The land is described as vomiting out its inhabitants, and the identical threat is pronounced over Israel herself in the same chapter — which is precisely what makes the conquest judicial rather than tribal. God did not favour Israel’s blood; He judged Canaan’s sin and warned Israel that her blood would not save her either. That warning was kept in 586 BC. A God who destroys Jericho and then exiles Jerusalem for the same offences is not a partisan deity.

The softer corruption is the Marcionite one that never announces itself: the practice of treating the Old Testament’s severity as a primitive layer that Jesus outgrew. Christ Himself said He came not to destroy the law and the prophets, and it is the Lamb of Revelation, not the Sinai lawgiver, who executes the final wrath. The proper answer to Canaan is not embarrassment but the Canaanite woman of Matthew 15:22, who received from Christ what her nation’s gods never gave, and Rahab, who is named in Hebrews 11 among the faithful. The line was never drawn by blood. It was drawn by faith, and it still is.
roots_summary: Hebrew Kena’an (H3667) is both a personal name and a land; Kena’ani (H3669) is the gentilic, the Canaanite, and in a second sense the merchant.
roots_lines: Hebrew Kena’an (H3667) — Canaan; the son of Ham (Genesis 9:22) and the land named for him.
Hebrew Kena’ani (H3669) — Canaanite; used both of the people (Genesis 15:21) and, by trade, of a merchant (Hosea 12:7).
Greek Chananaios (G5478) — Canaanitish; used of the woman of Matthew 15:22 whom Mark calls a Syrophenician.
The sevenfold list of Deuteronomy 7:1 sometimes contracts to six or expands to ten (Genesis 15:19-21); the number is representative, not a census.
In many texts Canaanite stands for the whole population of the land, with the six other names as its subdivisions.
usage: The iniquity of the Amorites is not yet full (Genesis 15:16) — the four-hundred-year forbearance that precedes the conquest.
Seven nations greater and mightier than thou (Deuteronomy 7:1) — the conquest is never presented as the strong overrunning the weak.
A woman of Canaan came out of the same coasts (Matthew 15:22) — the doomed nation supplies one of the great confessions of faith in the Gospels.

etymology: From Jebus, the old name of Jerusalem (Judges 19:10-11), itself from the personal name Jebus, third son of Canaan (Genesis 10:16). The Jebusites are the mountain people who held the ridge between the Kidron and the Tyropoeon valleys, and whose stronghold Israel could not take for four hundred years after Joshua.
biblical_def: The Jebusites are the people of Jebus, that is, of Jerusalem before it was Jerusalem. They stand in every list of the seven nations, and they are the standing monument to Israel’s unfinished obedience: the children of Judah could not drive them out (Joshua 15:63), and Benjamin did not either (Judges 1:21). For the whole period of the judges a Canaanite fortress sat in the middle of the inheritance, so unassailable that its garrison mocked David from the wall, saying the blind and the lame would keep him out (2 Samuel 5:6). Nevertheless David took the strong hold of Zion: the same is the city of David (2 Samuel 5:7). Then comes the turn that makes this entry more than military history. When David sinned in numbering Israel and the destroying angel stood over the city, the prophet Gad sent him to a Jebusite’s threshingfloor (2 Samuel 24:18). Araunah, called Ornan in Chronicles, offered his floor and his oxen freely; David refused to offer that which cost him nothing, and bought it. On that Jebusite threshingfloor Solomon built the house of the LORD (2 Chronicles 3:1). The last unconquered ground in Israel became the place of the altar, and then of the temple, and it is called mount Moriah.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 does not carry a separate JEBUSITE entry; the 1828 lexicon treats such gentilics under the general rule for proper nouns derived from a founder’s name, as it does with Canaanite.
webster_full: JEBUSITE, n. — A descendant of Jebus, the third son of Canaan; an inhabitant of Jebus, afterward Jerusalem.
The name of the city survives in Judges 19:10, Jebus, which is Jerusalem, and in 1 Chronicles 11:4.
Webster’s treatment of biblical gentilics is uniformly genealogical and geographical; the theological freight is left to the text.
The English form follows the Vulgate Jebusaeus through Wycliffe and Tyndale into the Authorized Version.
Where 1828 is silent, the King James translators are not: they render the term consistently across some forty occurrences, which is itself a lexical service.
scriptures: Joshua 15:63
As for the Jebusites the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the children of Judah could not drive them out: but the Jebusites dwell with the children of Judah at Jerusalem unto this day.
Judges 1:21
And the children of Benjamin did not drive out the Jebusites that inhabited Jerusalem; but the Jebusites dwell with the children of Benjamin in Jerusalem unto this day.
2 Samuel 5:7
Nevertheless David took the strong hold of Zion: the same is the city of David.
2 Samuel 24:18
And Gad came that day to David, and said unto him, Go up, rear an altar unto the LORD in the threshingfloor of Araunah the Jebusite.
2 Chronicles 3:1

Then Solomon began to build the house of the LORD at Jerusalem in mount Moriah, where the LORD appeared unto David his father, in the place that David had prepared in the threshingfloor of Ornan the Jebusite.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a tolerated remnant of sin does not stay quiet, and that God nevertheless plants His altar on the very ground His people failed to take.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. What needs recovering is the plain sense of Joshua 15:63 and Judges 1:21, two verses that record a failure and then repeat, twice, the phrase unto this day. The Holy Ghost has the chronicler note that the compromise outlived the generation that made it. Incomplete obedience is not a lesser obedience; it is a standing arrangement with what God said to remove, and it endures long after the men who arranged it are dead. Every pastor knows the domestic version of this: the sin not put to death in youth still holds its ridge in middle age, and its garrison still taunts from the wall.

The second thing to recover is the astonishing end of the story. God did not merely give David the fortress; He directed the altar to the threshingfloor of a Jebusite, and there Solomon raised the temple. The ground of longest resistance became the ground of atonement, and mount Moriah is where Abraham had already been told that God would provide Himself a lamb. Grace does not merely forgive the failure; it takes the very site of it and builds the house of sacrifice on it. That is the pattern of the gospel in a plot of threshing ground, and David’s refusal to offer that which doth cost me nothing is the right response to it.
roots_summary: Hebrew Yebusi (H2983), the Jebusite, from Yebus (H2982), Jebus — a name connected with the root bus, to tread down, fitting for both a threshingfloor and a trodden city.
roots_lines: Hebrew Yebus (H2982) — Jebus, the ancient name of Jerusalem (Judges 19:10; 1 Chronicles 11:4).
Hebrew Yebusi (H2983) — Jebusite; the gentilic used some forty times from Genesis 10:16 to Zechariah 9:7.
Hebrew bus (H947) — to tread down, to trample; the likely root behind the name.
Hebrew goren (H1637) — threshingfloor; Araunah’s floor in 2 Samuel 24:18 and the temple site of 2 Chronicles 3:1.
Araunah (2 Samuel 24) and Ornan (1 Chronicles 21) are the same man under two spellings, a common feature of the parallel histories.
usage: The children of Judah could not drive them out (Joshua 15:63) — the honest record of an unfinished conquest.
Nevertheless David took the strong hold of Zion (2 Samuel 5:7) — four centuries late, but taken.
In the threshingfloor of Ornan the Jebusite (2 Chronicles 3:1) — the last Canaanite ground becomes the temple mount.

etymology: From Midian, the fourth son of Abraham by Keturah (Genesis 25:2), whose descendants ranged the deserts east and south of the Gulf of Aqaba. Webster 1828 has no separate entry; the Authorized Version uses the form some sixty times, and the King James translators keep the older spelling Midianitish for the adjective in Numbers 25:6.
biblical_def: The Midianites are Abraham’s children by Keturah, and therefore Israel’s distant kin — which makes their history the more sobering. They are first seen as caravan traders who carry Joseph down into Egypt (Genesis 37:28, 36). Moses marries into them, and his father in law Jethro, priest of Midian, gives him the wisest civil counsel in the Pentateuch. Yet the same nation supplies the most successful assault ever made on Israel, and it was not made with the sword. At Shittim the daughters of Moab and Midian drew Israel into the sacrifices of their gods, and Israel joined himself unto Baalpeor (Numbers 25:3), and twenty and four thousand died of the plague. The LORD’s verdict names the method exactly: Vex the Midianites, and smite them: for they vex you with their wiles (Numbers 25:17-18). Wiles, not weapons. In the days of the judges Midian returns as a locust host with the Amalekites and the children of the east (Judges 6:33), and God breaks them with three hundred men and empty pitchers, having first stripped Gideon’s army down expressly lest Israel vaunt themselves against me (Judges 7:2). Isaiah remembers that night as the pattern of deliverance: the day of Midian.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 has no MIDIANITE entry, the lexicon being sparing with biblical gentilics; the sense is fixed entirely by the Authorized Version’s consistent usage from Genesis 37 to Isaiah 10.
webster_full: MIDIANITE, n. — A descendant of Midian, the son of Abraham by Keturah; one of the nomadic peoples of the Arabian desert east of the Red Sea.
Webster 1828 does not carry the word; the definition here follows the Authorized Version’s usage, which is uniform.
The adjective Midianitish appears in Numbers 25:6, 14, 15, 18 — an older English formation the King James translators preserved.
Isaiah 9:4 and 10:26 use the day of Midian as a byword for a deliverance God alone accomplished.
Where a gentilic is missing from 1828, the King James Version’s own steady rendering supplies the working definition.
scriptures: Genesis 37:28
Then there passed by Midianites merchantmen; and they drew and lifted up Joseph out of the pit, and sold Joseph to the Ishmeelites for twenty pieces of silver: and they brought Joseph into Egypt.
Numbers 25:3
And Israel joined himself unto Baalpeor: and the anger of the LORD was kindled against Israel.
Numbers 25:18

For they vex you with their wiles, wherewith they have beguiled you in the matter of Peor, and in the matter of Cozbi, the daughter of a prince of Midian, their sister, which was slain in the day of the plague for Peor’s sake.
Judges 6:33
Then all the Midianites and the Amalekites and the children of the east were gathered together, and went over, and pitched in the valley of Jezreel.
Judges 7:2
And the LORD said unto Gideon, The people that are with thee are too many for me to give the Midianites into their hands, lest Israel vaunt themselves against me, saying, Mine own hand hath saved me.
corruption_summary: The lesson of Midian is corrupted whenever the church expects the enemy to come as an enemy. Peor teaches that the assault which actually succeeds arrives as hospitality, a feast, and a marriage, not as an army.
corruption_paragraphs: Balaam could not curse Israel; Numbers 22 through 24 is four failed attempts and four blessings. So the counsel of Balaam, which Numbers 31:16 and Revelation 2:14 both name explicitly, changed the weapon. What no imprecation could do, an invitation did. The daughters of Moab and Midian called Israel to a feast, and the feast was to the gods, and the men who had crossed the Red Sea dry-shod bowed down. This is the single most instructive military fact in the Pentateuch, and the church has spent twenty centuries relearning it. Persecution has never emptied a congregation the way a comfortable alliance with the surrounding religion has.

The second corruption is the modern reading of Gideon’s three hundred as a leadership parable about elite teams and lean organizations. Judges 7:2 forecloses that reading in advance: the army was reduced lest Israel vaunt themselves against me. The reduction was not tactical wisdom; it was the removal of every ground of boasting, so that the victory could be attributed to no one but God. Every retelling that makes the three hundred a study in excellence has inverted the text. The pitchers were empty and the trumpets were not weapons. The sword of the LORD, and of Gideon — and in that order.
roots_summary: Hebrew Midyan (H4080), Midian, from a root din meaning strife or judgment; Midyani (H4084) is the gentilic.
roots_lines: Hebrew Midyan (H4080) — Midian; son of Abraham by Keturah (Genesis 25:2) and the land of his descendants.
Hebrew Midyani (H4084) — Midianite; the gentilic used through Numbers, Judges, and Isaiah.
Hebrew nekel (H5231) — wile, craft, subtlety; the word behind they vex you with their wiles (Numbers 25:18).
Hebrew Ba’al Pe’or (H1187) — Baalpeor, the lord of Peor, the Moabite-Midianite deity of Numbers 25:3.
Genesis 37 calls the traders both Midianites and Ishmeelites; the terms overlap for the desert caravan peoples descended from Abraham.
usage: They vex you with their wiles (Numbers 25:18) — the divine verdict on how Midian actually fought.
Lest Israel vaunt themselves against me (Judges 7:2) — why the army was made small.
Midianites merchantmen (Genesis 37:28) — the caravan that carried Joseph, and providence, down into Egypt.

etymology: From Ammon, short for Benammi, son of my people, the child born to Lot by his younger daughter (Genesis 19:38). The nation held the tableland east of the Jordan about Rabbah, and its god was Milcom, or Molech, whose worship required the passing of children through the fire.
biblical_def: The Ammonites descend from Lot by incest, and Scripture states the parentage plainly rather than hiding it: the younger, she also bare a son, and called his name Benammi: the same is the father of the children of Ammon unto this day (Genesis 19:38). Israel was forbidden to distress them in the wilderness, for their land was Lot’s inheritance, yet they were barred from the assembly: An Ammonite or Moabite shall not enter into the congregation of the LORD; even to their tenth generation (Deuteronomy 23:3), because they met Israel with hire against her rather than with bread. Their national character in the histories is cruelty dressed as diplomacy. Nahash the Ammonite would make a covenant with Jabeshgilead only on the condition that he thrust out every right eye and lay it for a reproach upon all Israel (1 Samuel 11:2), and it is on that provocation that the Spirit comes upon Saul. Their deeper harm was religious. Solomon built a high place for Molech, the abomination of the children of Ammon (1 Kings 11:7), and that altar stood before Jerusalem until Josiah defiled it. Nehemiah found Ammonite marriages in the restored community and named Solomon’s example as the warning (Nehemiah 13:23, 26). Zephaniah records their end: they reproached the LORD’s people and magnified themselves against their border.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 does not carry AMMONITE in its biblical sense; the 1828 lexicon reserves the word for the fossil shell named from the horn of Jupiter Ammon, which is a different word entirely.
webster_full: AMMONITE, n. — A descendant of Ben-ammi, the son of Lot; one of the people dwelling east of Jordan about Rabbah.
Webster 1828 does define AMMONITE, but as the spiral fossil shell called cornu Ammonis, the horn of Ammon — a mineralogical term unrelated to the biblical nation.
The biblical sense must therefore be taken from Scripture’s own consistent usage across some hundred occurrences.
The feminine Ammonitess appears of Naamah, the mother of Rehoboam (1 Kings 14:21, 31) — a marriage whose consequences ran through the divided kingdom.
That the same English word serves a fossil and a nation is a caution against reading a lexicon without its context.
scriptures: Genesis 19:38
And the younger, she also bare a son, and called his name Benammi: the same is the father of the children of Ammon unto this day.
Deuteronomy 23:3
An Ammonite or Moabite shall not enter into the congregation of the LORD; even to their tenth generation shall they not enter into the congregation of the LORD for ever:
1 Samuel 11:2
And Nahash the Ammonite answered them, On this condition will I make a covenant with you, that I may thrust out all your right eyes, and lay it for a reproach upon all Israel.
1 Kings 11:7
Then did Solomon build an high place for Chemosh, the abomination of Moab, in the hill that is before Jerusalem, and for Molech, the abomination of the children of Ammon.
Zephaniah 2:8
I have heard the reproach of Moab, and the revilings of the children of Ammon, whereby they have reproached my people, and magnified themselves against their border.
corruption_summary: Molech worship is treated by modern readers as a barbarism safely behind us, which is precisely the corruption: the god who required children remains the most successfully worshipped deity of the age, under names that sound like liberty.
corruption_paragraphs: Leviticus 20 does not describe Molech worship as a foreign curiosity but legislates against it inside Israel, because the temptation was live. The mechanism is what deserves attention. No one sacrificed a child for its own sake; children were given to Molech for prosperity, for security, for the future of the household. The god promised a better life in exchange for the life given. Any age that arranges its own convenience by the destruction of its offspring is not more advanced than Ammon; it has merely stopped building the altar in public. Solomon’s high place stood in the hill that is before Jerusalem — in full view of the temple, which is how these arrangements are always kept: openly, and with the worship of the true God continuing beside them.

The second thing to name is the exclusion of Deuteronomy 23:3 and how Scripture itself relieves it. The bar was covenantal, not racial, and the same canon that bars the Ammonite records Zelek the Ammonite among David’s mighty men (2 Samuel 23:37). Grace was never obliged to observe the fence God had built, and God has never been embarrassed by His own exceptions. But the exception is granted to the man who leaves Ammon and joins Israel, not to Ammon while it keeps Molech. That distinction is the whole difference between the gospel’s welcome and the modern demand that a church affirm what a man brings with him.
roots_summary: Hebrew Ammon (H5983) from Ben-Ammi (H1151), son of my people; the gentilic is Ammoni (H5984), and the god is Milcom (H4445) or Molech (H4432), from the root for king.
roots_lines: Hebrew Ben-Ammi (H1151) — son of my people; the name given by Lot’s younger daughter (Genesis 19:38).
Hebrew Ammon (H5983) — Ammon, the nation and its territory east of Jordan.
Hebrew Ammoni (H5984) — Ammonite; feminine Ammonith, Ammonitess, of Naamah (1 Kings 14:21).
Hebrew Molek (H4432) — Molech, from melek, king, pointed with the vowels of bosheth, shame, by the scribes.
Hebrew Milkom (H4445) — Milcom, the same deity under the fuller form of the name (1 Kings 11:5).
usage: The same is the father of the children of Ammon (Genesis 19:38) — Scripture names an ugly origin without flinching.
That I may thrust out all your right eyes (1 Samuel 11:2) — the terms Nahash called a covenant.
Molech, the abomination of the children of Ammon (1 Kings 11:7) — the god Solomon housed within sight of the temple.

etymology: From Moab, the son born to Lot by his elder daughter (Genesis 19:37), whose descendants held the plateau east of the Dead Sea between the Arnon and the Zered. Their god was Chemosh; their most famous daughter is Ruth; and their name is a permanent argument against reading Deuteronomy 23:3 as though blood were destiny.
biblical_def: The Moabites share an origin with Ammon in the cave above Zoar: the firstborn bare a son, and called his name Moab: the same is the father of the Moabites unto this day (Genesis 19:37). They are Israel’s kin and Israel’s snare. Balak king of Moab hired Balaam to curse Israel and could not buy a curse; then, by Balaam’s counsel, Moab did with a feast what could not be done with a prophecy: the people began to commit whoredom with the daughters of Moab (Numbers 25:1). For that hire and that seduction the law shut the assembly against them to the tenth generation (Deuteronomy 23:3). Yet the book of Ruth is set in the days of the judges and opens with Israelite men taking Moabite wives, and it ends with a Moabitess in the line of David and therefore of Christ. Ruth’s confession is the hinge: thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God (Ruth 1:16). Moab remains an enemy in the histories — Mesha’s revolt, the invading bands of 2 Kings 13:20 — and the prophets pronounce a heavy burden upon her for pride. But the genealogy at the end of Ruth stands in the canon as the standing proof that God can bring a daughter of Moab inside the very congregation His law had fenced.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 carries no MOABITE entry; as with the other biblical gentilics the sense is supplied by the Authorized Version, where the word occurs some fifty times from Genesis to Nehemiah.
webster_full: MOABITE, n. — A descendant of Moab, the son of Lot; an inhabitant of the highland east of the Dead Sea.
Webster 1828 omits the word; the King James Version’s uniform usage across Genesis, Deuteronomy, Ruth, Kings, and Nehemiah defines it sufficiently.
The feminine Moabitess is used five times of Ruth, and the title is never dropped — Boaz, the elders, and the narrator all keep it.
The plains of Moab (Numbers 22:1; Deuteronomy 34:8) are where the law was rehearsed and where Moses died within sight of the land.
That the narrator of Ruth insists on Ruth the Moabitess even after her marriage is deliberate: the reader is not allowed to forget where grace found her.
scriptures: Genesis 19:37
And the firstborn bare a son, and called his name Moab: the same is the father of the Moabites unto this day.
Numbers 25:1
And Israel abode in Shittim, and the people began to commit whoredom with the daughters of Moab.
Deuteronomy 23:3
An Ammonite or Moabite shall not enter into the congregation of the LORD; even to their tenth generation shall they not enter into the congregation of the LORD for ever:
Ruth 1:16

And Ruth said, Intreat me not to leave thee, or to return from following after thee: for whither thou goest, I will go; and where thou lodgest, I will lodge: thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God:
1 Kings 11:7
Then did Solomon build an high place for Chemosh, the abomination of Moab, in the hill that is before Jerusalem, and for Molech, the abomination of the children of Ammon.
corruption_summary: Ruth is regularly recruited as a text about inclusion, as though the point were that Israel should have been more welcoming. The book says something else: Ruth is received because Ruth renounces Chemosh and confesses the LORD.
corruption_paragraphs: The progressive reading of Ruth makes the Moabitess a case study in overcoming exclusionary law, with Boaz as the enlightened figure who sees past a bigoted statute. Every part of that reading fails on the text. The law of Deuteronomy 23:3 is God’s law, not a human prejudice for Boaz to transcend; the barrier is real, and Boaz honours it by pursuing the redemption legally, through the nearer kinsman and the elders at the gate. And Ruth is not admitted as a Moabitess retaining Moab. She says thy God my God, and she says it before she has any prospect of a husband, a field, or a son. What the book displays is conversion received into covenant, which is exactly what the church has always meant by the gospel, and exactly what the modern demand for affirmation is not.

The second corruption is the sentimental one that removes the horror from Numbers 25 in order to keep Ruth pleasant. The same nation supplies both narratives, and the canon puts them in the same Bible on purpose. Moab seduced Israel at Peor and Moab produced the great-grandmother of David. Neither fact cancels the other; together they teach that a people is not saved by its pedigree nor damned by it, and that God’s electing mercy runs where it will. Jacob have I loved, but Esau have I hated is the same doctrine seen from the other side.
roots_summary: Hebrew Moab (H4124), traditionally understood as from the father, a name that carries its own indictment; the gentilic is Moabi (H4125), feminine Moabiyyah, Moabitess.
roots_lines: Hebrew Moab (H4124) — Moab; the elder daughter’s son (Genesis 19:37) and the nation named for him.
Hebrew Moabi (H4125) — Moabite; feminine Moabiyyah, used of Ruth and of Solomon’s wives.
Hebrew Kemosh (H3645) — Chemosh, the abomination of Moab (1 Kings 11:7; Jeremiah 48:7).
Hebrew zanah (H2181) — to commit whoredom; used at Numbers 25:1 for a sin that was at once bodily and religious.
Numbers 22:1 places the plains of Moab as Israel’s last camp before Jordan — the whole of Deuteronomy is preached there.
usage: The same is the father of the Moabites unto this day (Genesis 19:37) — the origin Scripture refuses to conceal.
The people began to commit whoredom with the daughters of Moab (Numbers 25:1) — the seduction that succeeded where the curse failed.
Thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God (Ruth 1:16) — the confession that carried a Moabitess into the line of Christ.

etymology: From Edom, meaning red, the byname Esau earned over a bowl of red pottage (Genesis 25:30). Their land is the red rock country of Seir, south of the Dead Sea; the Greeks called it Idumea, and it is from that later Idumean line that the Herods came.
biblical_def: The Edomites are Esau’s children, and Scripture treats them as the near relation who behaves worst. These are the generations of Esau the father of the Edomites in mount Seir (Genesis 36:9). The law is remarkably tender toward them: Thou shalt not abhor an Edomite; for he is thy brother (Deuteronomy 23:7), and Israel was forbidden to take a foot of their land, because Seir was given to Esau as Canaan was given to Jacob. Yet Edom refused Israel passage on the King’s Highway, and the histories record a long enmity: Doeg the Edomite, the herdman of Saul, slaughtered eighty-five priests at Nob when no Israelite would lift a hand (1 Samuel 22:18); Hadad the Edomite was raised up as an adversary to Solomon. The prophets fix Edom’s guilt at one point above all others. When Jerusalem fell, Edom stood in the pass and cheered, and Obadiah’s whole prophecy answers it: For thy violence against thy brother Jacob shame shall cover thee, and thou shalt be cut off for ever (Obadiah 1:10). Ezekiel says the same, that Edom hath dealt against the house of Judah by taking vengeance. Malachi opens with the contrast Paul takes up in Romans 9, and the New Testament closes the account with Herod, an Idumean, seeking the life of the child born King of the Jews.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 has no EDOMITE entry; the name Edom is defined in the older gazetteers as red, and the Authorized Version’s usage across Genesis, Kings, Chronicles, and the prophets fixes the sense.
webster_full: EDOMITE, n. — A descendant of Esau, called Edom; an inhabitant of Mount Seir, south and east of the Dead Sea.
The name is from the Hebrew for red, given to Esau at Genesis 25:30 for the red pottage, and answering to the red sandstone of his country.
The Greek and Roman form is Idumean; 1 Maccabees and Josephus use it, and Mark 3:8 has Idumaea.
Webster 1828 does not carry the term; the definition follows Scripture and the standard geographies of Webster’s own century.
Herod the Great was an Idumean by descent, which is why Matthew 2 has an Edomite on the throne when the true Son of David is born.
scriptures: Genesis 36:9
And these are the generations of Esau the father of the Edomites in mount Seir:
Deuteronomy 23:7
Thou shalt not abhor an Edomite; for he is thy brother: thou shalt not abhor an Egyptian; because thou wast a stranger in his land.
1 Samuel 22:18

And the king said to Doeg, Turn thou, and fall upon the priests. And Doeg the Edomite turned, and he fell upon the priests, and slew on that day fourscore and five persons that did wear a linen ephod.
Obadiah 1:10
For thy violence against thy brother Jacob shame shall cover thee, and thou shalt be cut off for ever.
Romans 9:13
As it is written, Jacob have I loved, but Esau have I hated.
corruption_summary: Romans 9:13 is the verse most often explained away in the whole New Testament, usually by reducing God’s hatred of Esau to a Hebrew idiom for loving less — a move that empties Paul’s argument of the very thing he is arguing.
corruption_paragraphs: The standard evasion says that Esau have I hated is Semitic hyperbole for preference, and that the passage concerns nations rather than persons. Both halves fail. Paul has already anticipated the objection: he raises the choice before the twins were born, neither having done any good or evil, and he states the purpose, that the purpose of God according to election might stand, not of works, but of him that calleth. He then asks the question no merely national reading would provoke: Is there unrighteousness with God? Nobody asks that about a preference. The doctrine is unconditional election, and the Edomites are its historical illustration — a people descended from Abraham and Isaac, circumcised, near of kin, and passed by.

The other corruption runs opposite, and Christians fall into it more often: using Edom to sanctify grudges. Obadiah condemns Edom for standing in the crossway on the day of his brother’s calamity, for rejoicing over the children of Judah in the day of their destruction. That is a warning against gloating at a brother’s fall, and the Christian who reads Obadiah as permission to relish an enemy’s ruin has read himself into Edom’s part. The law’s own word stands over the whole account: Thou shalt not abhor an Edomite; for he is thy brother. God judged Edom. He did not hand the judgment over to Jacob.
roots_summary: Hebrew Edom (H123), red, from adom (H119) to be red; the gentilic is Adomi (H130); the land is Se’ir (H8165), hairy or shaggy, and Greek Idoumaia (G2401).
roots_lines: Hebrew Edom (H123) — red; the byname of Esau (Genesis 25:30) and the name of his nation.
Hebrew adom (H119) — to be red, ruddy; the same root behind Adam and the red earth.
Hebrew Adomi (H130) — Edomite; the gentilic, used of Doeg and of Hadad.
Hebrew Se’ir (H8165) — Seir, the mountain country of Edom, named for its shaggy or wooded slopes.
Greek Idoumaia (G2401) — Idumaea; the later name of the region (Mark 3:8), whence the Herodian house.
usage: Thou shalt not abhor an Edomite; for he is thy brother (Deuteronomy 23:7) — the law’s tenderness toward the nearest enemy.
Thy violence against thy brother Jacob (Obadiah 1:10) — the single charge on which Edom is condemned.
Jacob have I loved, but Esau have I hated (Romans 9:13) — the doctrine of election read out of Edom’s history.

etymology: From Egypt, in Hebrew Mitsrayim, a dual form usually understood of the two lands, Upper and Lower. Webster 1828 defines EGYPTIAN as a native of Egypt, and notes the secondary English sense of a gipsy, from the mistaken belief that the wandering people came out of Egypt.
biblical_def: The Egyptians are the first great world power the people of God encounter, and Scripture is careful never to flatten them into a single note. They are the house of bondage: the Egyptians made the children of Israel to serve with rigour (Exodus 1:13), and the cry of that oppression sets the Exodus in motion. They are also the refuge to which Abraham went in famine, into which Joseph was carried and over which he ruled, and in which Moses was raised so that he was learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians (Acts 7:22). At the Red Sea the LORD fought against them and they knew it: Let us flee from the face of Israel; for the LORD fighteth for them against the Egyptians (Exodus 14:25). Yet the plagues were not aimed at a race but at gods, and a mixed multitude went up with Israel. The law forbids contempt for them: thou shalt not abhor an Egyptian; because thou wast a stranger in his land (Deuteronomy 23:7). Isaiah goes further than any reader of Exodus would expect, prophesying an altar to the LORD in the midst of the land and a day when God says, Blessed be Egypt my people (Isaiah 19:25). And when the Son of God was in danger, Egypt sheltered Him, that it might be fulfilled, Out of Egypt have I called my son.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines EGYPTIAN as a native of Egypt, and as an adjective, pertaining to Egypt; he records the vulgar secondary sense of a gipsy, and the phrase Egyptian darkness for a darkness that can be felt, taken directly from Exodus 10:21.
webster_full: EGYPTIAN, a. — Pertaining to Egypt, in Africa.
EGYPTIAN, n. — A native of Egypt; also a gipsy, so called from the supposed origin of that wandering people.
Egyptian darkness — a thick palpable darkness, in allusion to the ninth plague, darkness which may be felt (Exodus 10:21).
Webster’s inclusion of the proverbial phrase shows how deeply the Exodus narrative had worked itself into ordinary English by 1828.
The gipsy sense is a historical error preserved in the language; the biblical sense is the only one Scripture knows.
scriptures: Exodus 1:13
And the Egyptians made the children of Israel to serve with rigour:
Exodus 14:27

And Moses stretched forth his hand over the sea, and the sea returned to his strength when the morning appeared; and the Egyptians fled against it; and the LORD overthrew the Egyptians in the midst of the sea.
Deuteronomy 23:7
Thou shalt not abhor an Edomite; for he is thy brother: thou shalt not abhor an Egyptian; because thou wast a stranger in his land.
Acts 7:22
And Moses was learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, and was mighty in words and in deeds.
Isaiah 19:25
Whom the LORD of hosts shall bless, saying, Blessed be Egypt my people, and Assyria the work of my hands, and Israel mine inheritance.
corruption_summary: The Exodus is the most frequently commandeered narrative in Scripture, made to serve every political liberation in turn while its own subject — a holy God redeeming a people to Himself for worship — is quietly dropped.
corruption_paragraphs: Liberation theology reads the Exodus as the paradigm of political emancipation, with Pharaoh standing for whatever structure the interpreter opposes and salvation consisting in the overthrow of it. The text will not carry that. God’s stated demand through Moses is not let my people go full stop, but let my people go, that they may serve me — the deliverance terminates in Sinai, in a covenant, in a tabernacle, and in a law. Israel was brought out of one service into another, and the second was the point. The moment the Exodus is severed from the worship it was for, it becomes a story about human autonomy, which is the precise opposite of what happened at the sea, where Israel was told to stand still and see the salvation of the LORD.

The narrower corruption is the reading of the plagues as an ethnic vendetta. Exodus 12:12 gives God’s own account: against all the gods of Egypt I will execute judgment. Each plague strikes at a deified thing — the Nile, the frog, the cattle, the sun — and the tenth strikes at the divine claim of Pharaoh’s own house. Meanwhile a mixed multitude leaves with Israel, Egyptians among them; the law commands kindness to the Egyptian sojourner by name; and Isaiah 19 ends with Egypt worshipping. The judgment fell on idolatry, not on blood, and the same principle explains both Canaan and Calvary.
roots_summary: Hebrew Mitsrayim (H4714), Egypt, a dual form; Mitsri (H4713) is the Egyptian; Greek Aigyptios (G124).
roots_lines: Hebrew Mitsrayim (H4714) — Egypt; a dual noun, commonly read of the two lands, Upper and Lower Egypt.
Hebrew Mitsri (H4713) — Egyptian; used of Hagar (Genesis 16:1) and of the taskmasters of Exodus 1.
Hebrew beth abadim — house of bondmen; the standing description of Egypt in Exodus 13:3 and Deuteronomy 5:6.
Greek Aigyptios (G124) — Egyptian; used at Acts 7:22, 24 and Hebrews 11:29.
In prophecy Egypt often stands for confidence in visible power, the bruised reed on which Judah leaned (2 Kings 18:21; Isaiah 36:6).
usage: The Egyptians made the children of Israel to serve with rigour (Exodus 1:13) — the bondage the Exodus answers.
Thou shalt not abhor an Egyptian (Deuteronomy 23:7) — the law forbids Israel a grudge against her old oppressor.
Blessed be Egypt my people (Isaiah 19:25) — the astonishing end of the prophetic account of Egypt.

etymology: The Authorized Version’s rendering of Hebrew Aram and its gentilic Arammi, the peoples of the highland north-east of Israel about Damascus, Zobah, and Maachah. Webster 1828 defines SYRIAN as pertaining to Syria, and notes the Syriac tongue, the Aramaic dialect in which portions of Ezra and Daniel are written.
biblical_def: The Syrians are the Aramean peoples of Damascus and the northern highlands, and Israel’s history with them is a long alternation of war, uneasy treaty, and startling grace. The bond is older than the enmity: the confession every Israelite made at the offering of firstfruits begins, A Syrian ready to perish was my father (Deuteronomy 26:5) — Jacob, who took his wives from Padanaram. David subdued them (2 Samuel 8:5-6); Benhadad and Hazael afterward pressed hard on Samaria; and the Syrian court supplies two of the most searching episodes in Kings. Their captains reasoned that Israel’s God was a god of the hills and not of the valleys (1 Kings 20:23), and were answered by a slaughter that taught the opposite. Their general Naaman, a great man and honourable and a leper, was sent to Jordan by a captive Israelite girl’s word, dipped seven times, and he was clean (2 Kings 5:14). Elisha’s servant, hemmed in by a Syrian host, had his eyes opened to see the mountain full of horses and chariots of fire. And when our Lord preached at Nazareth He chose this nation for His illustration of sovereign mercy: many lepers were in Israel in the time of Eliseus the prophet; and none of them was cleansed, saving Naaman the Syrian. They tried to kill Him for it.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines SYRIAN as a native of Syria and as pertaining to that country, and carries SYRIAC for the language — the dialect of Aramaic in which the Peshitta was written and in which portions of Ezra and Daniel stand.
webster_full: SYRIAN, a. — Pertaining to Syria; as the Syrian tongue.
SYRIAN, n. — A native of Syria.
SYRIAC, n. — The language of Syria; a dialect of the Aramean or Chaldee, in which the ancient Syriac version of the Scriptures was written.
2 Kings 18:26 records Hezekiah’s officers asking Rabshakeh to speak in the Syrian language, which they understood and the people on the wall did not.
The King James translators use Syrian where the Hebrew has Aram, following the Septuagint and Vulgate; modern versions often print Aram, which obscures the tie to Deuteronomy 26:5.
scriptures: Deuteronomy 26:5

And thou shalt speak and say before the LORD thy God, A Syrian ready to perish was my father, and he went down into Egypt, and sojourned there with a few, and became there a nation, great, mighty, and populous:
2 Samuel 8:6
Then David put garrisons in Syria of Damascus: and the Syrians became servants to David, and brought gifts. And the LORD preserved David whithersoever he went.
1 Kings 20:23

And the servants of the king of Syria said unto him, Their gods are gods of the hills; therefore they were stronger than we; but let us fight against them in the plain, and surely we shall be stronger than they.
2 Kings 6:17

And Elisha prayed, and said, LORD, I pray thee, open his eyes, that he may see. And the LORD opened the eyes of the young man; and he saw: and, behold, the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire round about Elisha.
Luke 4:27
And many lepers were in Israel in the time of Eliseus the prophet; and none of them was cleansed, saving Naaman the Syrian.
corruption_summary: Naaman’s cleansing is preached as a lesson in humility and rarely as what Christ made it — a proof of sovereign, discriminating mercy that so offended a synagogue it tried to throw the preacher off a cliff.
corruption_paragraphs: Luke 4:27 is Christ’s own commentary on the Naaman narrative, and He draws from it the doctrine of election: there were many lepers in Israel, and none of them was cleansed, saving the Syrian. The point is not that Naaman was more deserving, nor that God is broad-minded, but that mercy is God’s to give where He pleases, and He gave it past a nation full of covenant members to an enemy general. Nazareth understood Him perfectly, which is why the sermon ended with a mob and a hill. Where the doctrine is preached faithfully today it still gives offence, and where it gives no offence it is usually not being preached.

The lesser corruption is the therapeutic retelling in which Naaman’s difficulty is a matter of self-esteem and the servants are wise counsellors helping him process his resistance. The text is about authority. Naaman expected the prophet to come out and perform, and was given instead a bare word through a messenger and a muddy river. He was healed at the exact point where he stopped negotiating the terms of his own cleansing. That is the offence of the gospel in miniature, and no amount of pastoral warmth in the retelling should be allowed to soften it: wash, and be clean is a command, not a suggestion, and it is obeyed or it is not.
roots_summary: Hebrew Aram (H758), highland, the region the King James Version calls Syria; Arammi (H761) is the Syrian; Greek Syros (G4948).
roots_lines: Hebrew Aram (H758) — Aram, highland; rendered Syria throughout the Authorized Version.
Hebrew Arammi (H761) — Syrian, Aramean; the word behind a Syrian ready to perish was my father (Deuteronomy 26:5).
Hebrew Paddan Aram (H6307) — the plain of Aram, Rebekah’s and Rachel’s country (Genesis 28:2).
Hebrew aramith (H762) — in the Syrian tongue; Aramaic, the language of Ezra 4:8-6:18 and Daniel 2:4-7:28.
Greek Syros (G4948) — a Syrian; Luke 4:27 of Naaman. Mark 7:26 has Syrophenician for the woman of the coasts of Tyre.
usage: A Syrian ready to perish was my father (Deuteronomy 26:5) — every Israelite confessed a Syrian ancestor at the firstfruits.
Their gods are gods of the hills (1 Kings 20:23) — the Syrian theology God answered in the valley.
Saving Naaman the Syrian (Luke 4:27) — the text Christ preached to a congregation that tried to kill Him for it.

etymology: From Zidon, the King James spelling of Sidon, the ancient Phoenician harbour city on the coast north of Tyre, named in Genesis 10:15 for the firstborn of Canaan. The Authorized Version uses Zidon and Zidonians in the Old Testament and Sidon in the New, which conceals from the English reader that they are one place.
biblical_def: The Zidonians are the Phoenicians of the coast, the great seafarers and craftsmen of the ancient world, and Scripture records both what they gave Israel and what they cost her. They were among the oppressors of the days of the judges (Judges 10:12). They were also the workmen without whom the temple could not have been built: Solomon told Hiram plainly that there is not among us any that can skill to hew timber like unto the Sidonians (1 Kings 5:6), and the cedar of the second temple came the same way (Ezra 3:7). Their fatal gift was religious. Ahab took to wife Jezebel the daughter of Ethbaal king of the Zidonians, and went and served Baal, and worshipped him (1 Kings 16:31), and from that marriage came the slaughter of the prophets, Naboth’s vineyard, and the long contest of Elijah on Carmel. Solomon had already gone after Ashtoreth the goddess of the Zidonians. Yet the same coast holds one of the great scenes of mercy: it was to a widow of Zarephath, a city of Sidon, that Elijah was sent when there were many widows in Israel, and the Lord Jesus cited it beside Naaman. Christ Himself withdrew into those coasts, and there the Syrophenician mother received what she asked.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 carries no ZIDONIAN entry; the older geographies define Sidon as the mother city of Phoenicia, famed for glass, purple dye, navigation, and timber-work, and Scripture’s usage answers to that description exactly.
webster_full: ZIDONIAN, n. — An inhabitant of Zidon or Sidon, the Phoenician city on the Syrian coast; a Phoenician.
The name is Hebrew for fishing or fishery, from the trade by which the harbour first lived.
The Authorized Version writes Zidon in the Old Testament and Sidon in the New, following the Hebrew and the Greek respectively; the city is the same.
Sidon was celebrated in antiquity for glass-making, for the purple dye of the murex, and above all for timber-work and seamanship — all three appear in Scripture.
Webster 1828 does not treat biblical gentilics of this kind; the sense is fixed by 1 Kings, Ezra, and the Gospels.
scriptures: Judges 10:12
The Zidonians also, and the Amalekites, and the Maonites, did oppress you; and ye cried to me, and I delivered you out of their hand.
1 Kings 5:6

Now therefore command thou that they hew me cedar trees out of Lebanon; and my servants shall be with thy servants: and unto thee will I give hire for thy servants according to all that thou shalt appoint: for thou knowest that there is not among us any that can skill to hew timber like unto the Sidonians.
1 Kings 11:5
For Solomon went after Ashtoreth the goddess of the Zidonians, and after Milcom the abomination of the Ammonites.
1 Kings 16:31

And it came to pass, as if it had been a light thing for him to walk in the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, that he took to wife Jezebel the daughter of Ethbaal king of the Zidonians, and went and served Baal, and worshipped him.
Luke 4:26
But unto none of them was Elias sent, save unto Sarepta, a city of Sidon, unto a woman that was a widow.
corruption_summary: The Zidonian pattern is the church’s standing temptation: to hire the world’s craftsmen and then marry them. Skill is borrowed, and the religion comes with the skill unless a line is drawn on purpose.
corruption_paragraphs: Solomon was right that no Israelite could hew timber like a Sidonian, and it was no sin to hire them for the house of the LORD. The sin came later and by a different door: Solomon went after Ashtoreth the goddess of the Zidonians, and Ahab afterward married Ethbaal’s daughter. The sequence is worth naming because the modern church repeats it exactly. It borrows the world’s competence in music, marketing, therapy, and management — often with real justification, since the craft is genuine — and then finds it has also imported the anthropology that produced the craft. The regulative principle of worship exists precisely at this joint. What God has commanded is required in His worship; what He has not commanded is not admitted, however skilfully it is executed.

The second thing to see is that Sidon is not simply a cautionary tale. Elijah was fed there by a widow when Israel was starving, and Christ named it from the pulpit at Nazareth as evidence that God sends His mercy where He will. He went into those coasts Himself, and a mother of that country obtained her daughter’s deliverance by an argument built out of crumbs. The coast that gave Israel Jezebel also gave the Gospels one of the strongest confessions of faith recorded outside Israel. Nations are not fixed by their worst hour, and no reader should treat a people as beyond the reach of the mercy Christ deliberately preached to them.
roots_summary: Hebrew Tsidon (H6721), fishery, from tsud to hunt or fish; Tsidoni (H6722) is the Zidonian; Greek Sidon (G4605).
roots_lines: Hebrew Tsidon (H6721) — Zidon, Sidon; a fishery, from the harbour’s first trade.
Hebrew Tsidoni (H6722) — Zidonian, Sidonian; used of the workmen of 1 Kings 5:6 and the women of 1 Kings 11:1.
Hebrew Ashtoreth (H6252) — Ashtoreth, the goddess of the Zidonians (1 Kings 11:5), the Astarte of the Phoenicians.
Greek Sidon (G4605) — Sidon; paired with Tyre in the Gospels (Matthew 11:21; Mark 7:24).
Greek Sarepta (G4558) — Sarepta, the Zarephath of 1 Kings 17:9, a city of Sidon (Luke 4:26).
usage: Not among us any that can skill to hew timber like unto the Sidonians (1 Kings 5:6) — the world’s craft honestly acknowledged.
Jezebel the daughter of Ethbaal king of the Zidonians (1 Kings 16:31) — the marriage that cost Israel a century.
Save unto Sarepta, a city of Sidon (Luke 4:26) — mercy sent past Israel to a Zidonian widow.

etymology: From Hebrew Chori, commonly derived from chor, a hole or cave — hence cave-dwellers, the troglodytes of the sandstone country of Seir. Deuteronomy calls them Horims. They are the aboriginal inhabitants of Edom, dispossessed by the children of Esau exactly as Canaan was afterward dispossessed by the children of Jacob.
biblical_def: The Horites are the first people named as dwelling in mount Seir, the cave country south of the Dead Sea. Chedorlaomer smote the Horites in their mount Seir on his sweep through the region in Abraham’s day (Genesis 14:6), and Genesis 36 preserves their genealogy alongside Esau’s: These are the sons of Seir the Horite, who inhabited the land (Genesis 36:20), with their dukes named man by man. Then they vanish. Deuteronomy records how, and the record is the reason this small people belongs in a dictionary at all: The Horims also dwelt in Seir beforetime; but the children of Esau succeeded them, when they had destroyed them from before them, and dwelt in their stead; as Israel did unto the land of his possession, which the LORD gave unto them (Deuteronomy 2:12). Moses draws the comparison himself. The same God who was then giving Canaan to Israel had earlier given Seir to Esau, and Ar to Moab, and the Caphtorim’s land to those who took it. Amos states the principle bluntly, that the God who brought Israel out of Egypt also brought the Philistines from Caphtor and the Syrians from Kir. The Horites are Scripture’s quiet proof that the nations are moved about the earth by one hand.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 carries no HORITE entry. The definition follows the Hebrew root for a cave and Scripture’s own account in Genesis 14, Genesis 36, and Deuteronomy 2 — the last of which supplies the theological point.
webster_full: HORITE, n. — A cave-dweller; one of the aboriginal inhabitants of Mount Seir, dispossessed by the children of Esau.
The name is usually derived from Hebrew chor, a hole or cavern, the sandstone of Seir being honeycombed with dwellings cut in the rock.
Deuteronomy 2:12 and 2:22 use the form Horims; Genesis uses Horites and Horite.
Genesis 36 gives their dukes by name, the only such record of an extinguished people preserved in the canon beside the people who replaced them.
Webster 1828 does not treat the word; the sense is entirely biblical and geographical.
scriptures: Genesis 14:6
And the Horites in their mount Seir, unto Elparan, which is by the wilderness.
Genesis 36:20
These are the sons of Seir the Horite, who inhabited the land; Lotan, and Shobal, and Zibeon, and Anah,
Deuteronomy 2:12

The Horims also dwelt in Seir beforetime; but the children of Esau succeeded them, when they had destroyed them from before them, and dwelt in their stead; as Israel did unto the land of his possession, which the LORD gave unto them.
Deuteronomy 2:22
As he did to the children of Esau, which dwelt in Seir, when he destroyed the Horims from before them; and they succeeded them, and dwelt in their stead even unto this day:
Amos 9:7

Are ye not as children of the Ethiopians unto me, O children of Israel? saith the LORD. Have not I brought up Israel out of the land of Egypt? and the Philistines from Caphtor, and the Syrians from Kir?
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the doctrine of Deuteronomy 2 — that God assigns and removes the habitations of every nation, not Israel’s only, and that no people holds its ground by right of blood or arms.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. What the Horites recover for us is a doctrine the modern mind resists in both directions. Deuteronomy 2 says that God gave Seir to Esau by dispossessing the Horites, gave Ar to the children of Lot by dispossessing the Emims, and gave Canaan to Israel by dispossessing the Amorites. Paul states the same in Athens: God hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation. The secular reading sees only migration, conquest, and demography, with no hand behind them. The sentimental religious reading sees God’s providence over Israel alone, as though the other nations moved by accident. Scripture says otherwise, and says it about a people whose name survives in four verses.

There is a second use, and it is pastoral. The Horites had dukes, genealogies, and a country cut into living rock, and they are gone; the canon preserves their names in a chapter mostly given to Esau’s. Nothing a nation builds secures its tenure. The land itself is the LORD’s, and every occupant is a tenant. That truth cut against Israel, who was warned in the same book that she would be plucked off the land for the same abominations, and it cuts against every people that assumes its own permanence. Only one kingdom in Scripture is promised that it cannot be moved, and it is not held by any nation on earth.
roots_summary: Hebrew Chori (H2752), Horite, from chor (H2356), a hole or cave; Se’ir (H8165) is their mountain country, afterward Edom.
roots_lines: Hebrew Chori (H2752) — Horite, Horim; the cave-dwelling people of Seir.
Hebrew chor (H2356) — a hole, a cave; the likely root, answering to the rock-cut dwellings of the region.
Hebrew Se’ir (H8165) — Seir; the mountain country the Horites held and Esau took.
Hebrew yarash (H3423) — to dispossess, to succeed to a possession; the verb of Deuteronomy 2:12 and of Israel’s own conquest.
Genesis 36:20-30 lists their dukes: Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon, Anah, Dishon, Ezer, and Dishan — a preserved record of a people otherwise lost.
usage: The Horites in their mount Seir (Genesis 14:6) — their one appearance in the narrative of Abraham’s day.
The children of Esau succeeded them, and dwelt in their stead (Deuteronomy 2:12) — the dispossession God Himself ordered.
As Israel did unto the land of his possession (Deuteronomy 2:12) — Moses compares Israel’s conquest to Esau’s, under one providence.
